tagline.text: A hands-on children's museum in the old Elks Club on Roxas Boulevard

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of Roxas Boulevard and South Drive, Ermita, Manila (former Elks Club building)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Year-round (indoors), dry season December–May for walks nearby

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱150–450 (per person, admission varies by source, transport extra)

children.text: Museo Pambata is the first hands-on children's museum in the Philippines, opened in 1994 in the former Elks Club building on Roxas Boulevard in Manila. It closed in 2020 and reopened after renovation in December 2024, with eight themed rooms where children learn through play.

Museo Pambata is a Tagalog name meaning "children's museum," and it is presented as the first interactive children's museum in the Philippines. It stands at the corner of Roxas Boulevard and South Drive in the Ermita district of Manila, close to Rizal Park and Manila Bay, and it is a regular stop for families spending a day in Manila with children. The building is the former Elks Club, built in 1910, so it is a piece of old Manila in itself and worth seeing even for adults.

The museum's story goes back to 1993. Early childhood educator Nina Lim-Yuson, inspired by the Boston Children's Museum, proposed the idea with her mother, Estefania Aldaba-Lim, to Manila Mayor Alfredo Lim, and a board of trustees was formed that June. In December of the same year the Manila City Council approved a 10-year rent-free lease, and the museum officially opened on December 21, 1994. For about 30 years since, it has served as a place where Filipino children learn about the environment, history, careers and the human body through play.

The exhibits are divided into eight themed rooms. They include Kalikasan and Karagatan, which introduce forests and the sea, Maynila Noon, a recreation of old Manila, Paglaki Ko, where children try out what they want to be when they grow up, Pamilihang Bayan, a market play area, Katawan Ko, which explores the structure of the body, Bata sa Mundo, about children in the world, a room about how to love planet Earth, and Tuklas, a hands-on room for science, technology, engineering and math (STEM). There are also a children's library, a changing exhibits hall, a gift shop and a playground. The 2024 reopening is said to have added a rock-climbing wall and a Bahay na Bato corner about the traditional Filipino house. Some announcements also mention spaces such as Karapatan Hall about children's rights, a Classroom of the Future for digital learning, Isla Pambata about the lives and culture of Filipino children, and Himig and Habi on music and weaving. Which spaces are actually open varies over time, so check the guide map when you arrive.

Museo Pambata closed in 2020 because of COVID-19 and, after extensive renovation, reopened on December 6, 2024 for its 30th anniversary. Right after the reopening, the first floor opened first and the remaining exhibits were opened in stages, so it is a good idea to check which exhibits are open before you go. Opening hours and fees differ by source, so this guide gives only ranges. It fits well into a half-day plan for families traveling in Manila with children. Many of the exhibits are easy to follow in English, so even children not used to English can join in through hands-on play. Many families in Manila combine it with Intramuros or the National Museum area for a full day. As a children's museum it is not really a place for adults on their own, but it is a good way to introduce a niece, nephew or your own children to old Manila and Philippine culture.

These rooms recreate a tropical rainforest and the sea with models, introducing the variety of Philippine nature at a child's eye level. The Under the Sea area in the lobby is said to have a whale shark installation.
This room recreates Spanish-era streets, a tranvia (tram) and a galleon. Children can see old Manila and climb aboard, so it pairs well with a trip to Intramuros.
A career role-play room and a market play room. By playing doctors, firefighters and shopkeepers, children learn how society works through play.
A room about the body's structure and health, where children touch and press things to learn about organs and the senses.
A room where children look at toys and dolls from many countries to learn about cultural differences. If you visit with foreign children, it is fun to compare how each plays.

A hands-on room for science experiments and STEM. Older elementary children stay here the longest, so if time is short, see this room first. A changing exhibit space curated by young people, Balay Yatu, is also known, so it is worth seeing what is on during your visit.

With a library for reading and a playground, it is a good place for children tired from the exhibits to rest. A rock-climbing wall was also added at the 2024 reopening. Play zones named Bahay Pukyutan and Tutubing Bakal are also mentioned, which are comfortable for families with younger siblings.
A corner introducing the traditional Filipino house, where you can look at the structure of old homes and everyday tools. It is also a place where Filipino children learn about their own culture.

items.title: Half-day route with children
items.subtitle: The museum and a walk on Roxas Boulevard

children.text: Take a taxi or Grab from your hotel to the corner of Roxas Boulevard and South Drive and enter when it opens. Check at the information desk which exhibits are open.
Start with the room your child will find most interesting. The environment room and the old Manila room are good for photos.
Rest in the museum's rest area and have lunch at a nearby restaurant.
Finish the science room, the library and the playground.
After your visit, walk to Rizal Park or toward Manila Bay and enjoy an evening stroll at sunset.
An announcement said two-hour activities are held at set times on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Check the museum's social media for the latest schedule.
Start on foot at Bahay Tsinoy or San Agustin Church in Intramuros.
Have lunch at a restaurant inside Intramuros.
Take a taxi to Museo Pambata on Roxas Boulevard and give your child time to run around.
Walk around nearby Rizal Park and enjoy the Manila Bay sunset on foot, then have dinner at a restaurant in the city.
Return to your hotel by Grab and have dinner and rest. If your child is tired, finish early.
It takes about
40 minutes to 1 hour 30 minutes
by taxi or Grab from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) to the museum, depending heavily on the time of day.
If you are staying in Ermita or Malate, it is often within
5–15 minutes
by taxi.
The exact time varies with traffic, so leave with time to spare.
The nearest LRT-1 station is said to be UN Avenue Station. Walk from the station to the museum or take a short taxi ride.
The walk from the station is hot and the traffic is heavy, so a taxi is recommended if you are with children.
UN Avenue Station is said to be close to the National Museum area, so if you plan to see both museums, you can also continue on foot from near the station. Check the walking sections with a map app.
You can reach Roxas Boulevard by jeepney, bus, taxi or Grab. The museum is on a main road, so watch for vehicles when you get out.
Sights such as the National Museum, Rizal Park, Intramuros and Manila Ocean Park are close, so it is easy to continue by taxi.
It is an indoor museum, so you can go any time of year. It is also a good way to spend time with children on a rainy day.
It tends to be crowded on weekends and school holidays. For a quiet visit, choose a weekday morning, but opening days and hours can change, so check before you go.

An announcement said commemorative events and Christmas-season programs were held at the end of the reopening year. Weekdays with many school field trips can be crowded with groups, so families may want to ask the museum which times have fewer group visits.

There are many hotels around Ermita and Malate, a short taxi ride from the museum. Families can also base themselves near Manila Bay on the west side of the city or in Makati. Prices and reviews change from season to season, so check them on a booking site.

The museum is said to have a cafe and a gift shop. Food may be eaten only in designated areas, so check the rules. Ermita and Malate nearby have Korean and Japanese restaurants, Filipino restaurants and mall food courts, so lunch is easy. The museum is also said to offer facilities such as rest areas, drinking water, first aid and lockers for breaks during your visit. The building has ramps and elevators, making it easy to move around with a stroller or wheelchair, and accessible restrooms are said to be available.

Before you go, check on the museum's social media which rooms are open, plus the hours and fees. Some announcements say it is open Tuesday to Sunday and others say mainly Friday to Sunday, so checking the day before is safest.
Dress children in comfortable clothes and sneakers for active play.
Bringing water and hand sanitizer is handy.
Activity programs at set times may be held from Friday to Sunday, so check the schedule.
Reserve group visits and guided tours in advance.
Midday is hot and the sun is strong, so wear a hat when moving around outside the museum.
Keep your wallet and phone on you and do not let go of your child's hand.
On days when you combine Rizal Park and Intramuros, split the museum into a morning or an afternoon visit to pace your energy.
The gift shop is said to sell Filipino children's books and toys, so leave time in your plan to choose souvenirs.
The museum is reported to be opening its exhibits in stages after the reopening, so be sure to check the open rooms, hours and fees before you go.
Hours and fees differ by source, so you may make the trip for nothing. The information in this guide is what could be confirmed in 2026.
Announcements say food is allowed only in designated areas, so check the rules. Play facilities for children may have age and height limits for safety, so follow the on-site instructions.
Roxas Boulevard has heavy traffic, so use the signals and crosswalks when crossing with children.
The museum may be closed on Mondays and public holidays, so check the day before.
Manila's best-known park, close to the museum and good for strolls and photos.
A museum complex in and around Rizal Park, easy to pair with your museum tour.
The Spanish-era walled city a short taxi ride away, with churches and a fort to explore.
A marine life attraction that is a good place to visit with children.
